summary.text: A 52-year old Caucasian man previously treated for alcohol abuse was found by a local doctor having an epileptic seizure, which stopped after diazepam 10 mg. The emergency doctor found him unconscious, bradypnoeic at 6 breaths/min and cyanotic; he underwent rapid sequence intubation, had narrow pupils and salivation during transport, and head CT and chest X-ray were normal. On ICU admission about 2 h after the seizure he had excessive perspiration and diarrhoea without other muscarinic signs, and was haemodynamically stabilised after fluid resuscitation.

Initial laboratory tests showed leucocytosis, hyperglycaemia, high creatine kinase, hyperlactataemia, hypokalaemia, acidosis with pH 7.08 and low serum ChE; urine toxicology screen and serum alcohol were negative. Tracheal aspirate grew three organisms and amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, started empirically for possible aspiration pneumonia, was continued. Carbofuran was identified in urine and carbofuran with chlormephos in gastric fluid, matching a purple powder found by relatives.

Obidoxime was started intravenously about 10 h after admission as a 250 mg bolus then a 750 mg infusion over 24 h, with standard intensive care medication and thiamine; atropine was not used. Additional short-term seizures in the first eight hours were managed with lorazepam and no further seizures followed obidoxime. EEG was abnormal; a neurologist was consulted and no further imaging was done. Serial ChE, lactate, CRP, leucocytes, potassium and creatine kinase over three days are in Table 1.

The patient improved on oxime therapy without adverse reactions; one day after it was stopped plasma ChE rose and he was gradually extubated. After five days a psychiatrist found symptoms of depression and a possible suicide attempt, which he denied; he was transferred to the psychiatry ward, and later reported that he intentionally drank the poison because his wife had left him a month earlier.

ambiguities.issue: The neurologist concluded the seizures were due to metabolic causes, while the authors state they do not believe any condition other than poisoning could have provoked the seizures.

evidence.quote: A neurologist was consulted, who concluded that the seizures were due to metabolic causes, so no further imaging was done.
We do not believe the patient has had any other indications or conditions that could provoke seizures other than poisoning.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not resolve whether the metabolic cause is separate from or part of the poisoning.

ambiguities.issue: Route and amount of exposure differ between accounts: relatives thought he could have drunk the powder with his morning coffee and did not know the amount; the patient later said he intentionally drank some 30-year-old poison.

evidence.quote: They did not know how much was ingested but thought that he could have drunk it with his morning coffee.
Some time after his transfer to psychiatry, he reported that he intentionally drank some 30-year-old poison, because his wife left him a month earlier and he wanted to die.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not assume the coffee route, the amount, or that the 30-year-old poison is the powder found at home.

ambiguities.issue: The psychiatrist reported a possibility of suicide attempt which the patient denied at the time; he later reported intentional ingestion.
